--- title: "Predictive Modeling" subtitle: "ML Methods for AI vs. Non-AI Career Analysis (PySpark MLlib)" author: - name: Maria Taylor affiliations: - id: bu name: Boston University city: Boston state: MA date: "2026-06-14" bibliography: references.bib csl: csl/econometrica.csl format: html: toc: true number-sections: true df-print: paged execute: freeze: auto --- ## Overview This section applies machine learning models to the 2024 Lightcast job postings dataset to analyze AI vs. Non-AI career patterns using **PySpark MLlib**. Two approaches are used: **KMeans Clustering** (unsupervised) to discover natural job groupings, and **Logistic Regression + Random Forest** (supervised) to predict whether a job is AI-related. ::: {#d74195fb .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import pandas as pd import numpy as np import plotly.express as px import plotly.graph_objects as go import plotly.io as pio import re from pyspark.sql import SparkSession from pyspark.sql.functions import col, udf, when, avg from pyspark.sql.types import IntegerType from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, VectorAssembler, StandardScaler, PCA from pyspark.ml.clustering import KMeans from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier from pyspark.ml.evaluation import ClusteringEvaluator from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix pio.templates.default = "plotly_white" spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("MLMethods").config("spark.ui.showConsoleProgress", "false").getOrCreate() spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR") sdf = (spark.read .option("header", "true") .option("inferSchema", "true") .option("multiLine", "true") .option("escape", "\"") .csv("cleaned_lightcast_jobs.csv")) sdf = sdf.filter((col("SOC_2021_5") != "Unknown") & (col("TITLE_RAW") != "Unknown")) sdf = sdf.fillna(0, subset=["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE", "MIN_EDULEVELS"]) print(f"Dataset shape: ({sdf.count()}, {len(sdf.columns)})") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` WARNING: Using incubator modules: jdk.incubator.vector Using Spark's default log4j profile: org/apache/spark/log4j2-defaults.properties Setting default log level to "WARN". To adjust logging level use sc.setLogLevel(newLevel). For SparkR, use setLogLevel(newLevel). 26/06/21 14:37:30 WARN NativeCodeLoader: Unable to load native-hadoop library for your platform... using builtin-java classes where applicable ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Dataset shape: (51245, 82) ``` ::: ::: ## Creating the AI Job Indicator Following the same methodology established in the Data Cleaning section, jobs are classified as AI-related using keyword matching on title and skill fields. ::: {#1b19c372 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ai_keywords_exact = [ r"\bai\b", r"\bllm\b", r"\bmlops\b", r"\bnlp\b", r"\bml engineer\b", r"\btensorflow\b", r"\bpytorch\b" ] ai_keywords_partial = [ "artificial intelligence", "machine learning", "deep learning", "data scientist", "generative ai", "reinforcement learning", "computer vision", "large language model", "predictive modeling", "natural language processing", "neural network", "data science", "data engineer", "data analyst", "statistical modeling", "predictive analytics", "business intelligence" ] def is_ai(title): t = str(title).lower() for kw in ai_keywords_exact: if re.search(kw, t): return 1 for kw in ai_keywords_partial: if kw in t: return 1 return 0 is_ai_udf = udf(is_ai, IntegerType()) sdf = sdf.withColumn("AI_JOB", is_ai_udf(col("TITLE_RAW"))) sdf.cache() ai_counts = sdf.groupBy("AI_JOB").count().orderBy("AI_JOB").toPandas() ai_counts.columns = ["AI Job", "Count"] ai_counts["AI Job"] = ai_counts["AI Job"].map({0: "Non-AI", 1: "AI-Related"}) print(ai_counts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AI Job Count 0 Non-AI 36731 1 AI-Related 14514 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#c6ec29ae .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = px.pie( ai_counts, names="AI Job", values="Count", title="Distribution of AI vs. Non-AI Job Postings", color="AI Job", color_discrete_map={"AI-Related": "#e74c3c", "Non-AI": "#3498db"} ) fig.update_layout( font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), legend_title="Career Type" ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Insight:** AI-related positions represent approximately 28% of all job postings in the dataset, capturing data science, analytics, business intelligence, and machine learning roles. This broader definition reflects the true scope of AI-adjacent careers in the 2024 labor market. ## KMeans Clustering KMeans clustering groups job postings based on occupational characteristics — experience requirements, education level, and SOC classification — to identify whether AI-related jobs form distinct natural clusters. A data quality issue was identified during feature preparation: the `MIN_EDULEVELS` field uses the code **99 to mean "No Education Listed"** — a missing-data flag rather than a true ordinal education level. Left uncorrected, this placeholder distorts distance-based clustering. We replace it with the median of valid education levels before clustering. ::: {#2d43cadc .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} valid_edu = sdf.filter(col("MIN_EDULEVELS") != 99) median_edu = valid_edu.approxQuantile("MIN_EDULEVELS", [0.5], 0.01)[0] sdf = sdf.withColumn( "MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN", when(col("MIN_EDULEVELS") == 99, median_edu).otherwise(col("MIN_EDULEVELS")) ) print(f"Median valid education level used for imputation: {median_edu}") indexer_soc = StringIndexer(inputCol="SOC_2021_5", outputCol="SOC_ENC", handleInvalid="keep") indexer_onet = StringIndexer(inputCol="ONET", outputCol="ONET_ENC", handleInvalid="keep") sdf = indexer_soc.fit(sdf).transform(sdf) sdf = indexer_onet.fit(sdf).transform(sdf) cluster_features = ["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE", "MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN", "SOC_ENC"] assembler = VectorAssembler(inputCols=cluster_features, outputCol="features_raw") sdf_vec = assembler.transform(sdf) scaler = StandardScaler(inputCol="features_raw", outputCol="features", withMean=True, withStd=True) scaler_model = scaler.fit(sdf_vec) sdf_scaled = scaler_model.transform(sdf_vec).cache() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Median valid education level used for imputation: 2.0 ``` ::: ::: ### Elbow Method and Silhouette Score To determine the optimal number of clusters, we evaluate KMeans across k = 2 to 7 using both **inertia (elbow method)** and **silhouette score**. ::: {#7e5761ec .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} evaluator = ClusteringEvaluator(featuresCol="features", predictionCol="prediction") elbow_rows = [] for k in range(2, 8): km = KMeans(featuresCol="features", k=k, seed=42) model = km.fit(sdf_scaled) cost = model.summary.trainingCost preds = model.transform(sdf_scaled) sil = evaluator.evaluate(preds) elbow_rows.append({"k": k, "Inertia": cost, "Silhouette": sil}) elbow_df = pd.DataFrame(elbow_rows) print(elbow_df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` k Inertia Silhouette 0 2 61033.170034 0.835087 1 3 30113.318675 0.803789 2 4 25791.192762 0.743782 3 5 18840.199306 0.720179 4 6 13343.671097 0.795845 5 7 12028.902515 0.792499 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4c50bf84 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = px.line( elbow_df, x="k", y="Inertia", markers=True, title="Elbow Method: Inertia vs. Number of Clusters", color_discrete_sequence=["#3498db"] ) fig.update_layout(font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), height=400) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#052a5a9f .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = px.line( elbow_df, x="k", y="Silhouette", markers=True, title="Silhouette Score vs. Number of Clusters", color_discrete_sequence=["#e74c3c"] ) fig.update_layout(font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), height=400) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Insight:** The elbow method shows the steepest drop in inertia between k=2 and k=3, after which the curve flattens substantially — the classic elbow point. While k=2 has the single highest silhouette score (0.835), k=3 retains a strong silhouette (0.804) while providing a richer, more interpretable three-way segmentation. **k=3 is selected** as the optimal number of clusters. ::: {#5319586c .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} kmeans = KMeans(featuresCol="features", predictionCol="Cluster", k=3, seed=42) kmeans_model = kmeans.fit(sdf_scaled) sdf_clustered = kmeans_model.transform(sdf_scaled).cache() cluster_profile = sdf_clustered.groupBy("Cluster").agg( avg("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE").alias("Avg_Experience"), avg("MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN").alias("Avg_Education"), avg("AI_JOB").alias("Pct_AI") ).orderBy("Cluster").toPandas() cluster_size = sdf_clustered.groupBy("Cluster").count().orderBy("Cluster").toPandas() cluster_profile = cluster_profile.merge(cluster_size, on="Cluster") print(cluster_profile) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cluster Avg_Experience Avg_Education Pct_AI count 0 0 4.327045 2.030315 0.317346 39386 1 1 10.180003 1.990579 0.109157 7961 2 2 4.370190 0.305028 0.293997 3898 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#6a37cb7b .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_df = cluster_profile.copy() plot_df["Cluster"] = plot_df["Cluster"].astype(str) fig = px.bar( plot_df.sort_values("Cluster"), x="Cluster", y="count", title="Distribution of Job Clusters Identified by KMeans", labels={"Cluster": "Cluster ID", "count": "Number of Job Postings"}, color="Cluster", color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Bold, category_orders={"Cluster": ["0", "1", "2"]} ) fig.update_layout( font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), showlegend=False, height=450 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Insight:** Cluster 0 is the dominant group (76.9% of postings, ~4.3 years experience, ~Bachelor's education). Cluster 1 represents senior/experienced roles (15.5%, ~10.2 years experience), and Cluster 2 represents lower-formal-education roles (7.6%, ~Associate's or below). Experience — not education — is the primary axis separating these groups. ::: {#b7e3673e .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} ai_cluster = sdf_clustered.groupBy("Cluster", "AI_JOB").count().toPandas() ai_cluster["Type"] = ai_cluster["AI_JOB"].map({0: "Non-AI", 1: "AI-Related"}) ai_cluster["Cluster"] = ai_cluster["Cluster"].astype(str) fig = px.bar( ai_cluster, x="Cluster", y="count", color="Type", barmode="stack", title="AI vs. Non-AI Distribution per Cluster", labels={"Cluster": "Cluster ID", "count": "Job Postings"}, color_discrete_map={"AI-Related": "#e74c3c", "Non-AI": "#3498db"}, category_orders={"Cluster": ["0", "1", "2"]} ) fig.update_layout( font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), height=450 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Insight:** AI job density is highest in Cluster 0 (31.7%) and Cluster 2 (29.4%) — both lower-experience groups — but drops sharply in Cluster 1 (10.9%), the senior/high-experience group. This suggests AI-related roles skew toward earlier-career positions rather than senior traditional roles, regardless of formal education level. ### PCA Visualization (Interactive) To visualize the cluster structure in two dimensions, we project the scaled features onto their first two principal components. Use the dropdown below to toggle between coloring by **Cluster** or by **AI Job Status**. ::: {#177bd0c3 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} pca = PCA(k=2, inputCol="features", outputCol="pca_features") pca_model = pca.fit(sdf_clustered) sdf_pca = pca_model.transform(sdf_clustered) print(f"Explained variance (PC1, PC2): {pca_model.explainedVariance}") pca_sample = sdf_pca.select("pca_features", "Cluster", "AI_JOB").sample(0.1, seed=42).toPandas() pca_sample["PC1"] = pca_sample["pca_features"].apply(lambda v: float(v[0])) pca_sample["PC2"] = pca_sample["pca_features"].apply(lambda v: float(v[1])) pca_sample["Cluster"] = pca_sample["Cluster"].astype(str) pca_sample["AI_Status"] = pca_sample["AI_JOB"].map({0: "Non-AI", 1: "AI-Related"}) cluster_colors = {"0": "#3498db", "1": "#e74c3c", "2": "#2ecc71"} ai_colors = {"Non-AI": "#3498db", "AI-Related": "#e74c3c"} fig = go.Figure() cluster_ids = sorted(pca_sample["Cluster"].unique()) for c in cluster_ids: sub = pca_sample[pca_sample["Cluster"] == c] fig.add_trace(go.Scatter( x=sub["PC1"], y=sub["PC2"], mode="markers", name=f"Cluster {c}", marker=dict(color=cluster_colors.get(c, "#888"), opacity=0.5, size=6), visible=True )) for status in ["Non-AI", "AI-Related"]: sub = pca_sample[pca_sample["AI_Status"] == status] fig.add_trace(go.Scatter( x=sub["PC1"], y=sub["PC2"], mode="markers", name=status, marker=dict(color=ai_colors[status], opacity=0.5, size=6), visible=False )) n_cluster_traces = len(cluster_ids) n_ai_traces = 2 cluster_visibility = [True]*n_cluster_traces + [False]*n_ai_traces ai_visibility = [False]*n_cluster_traces + [True]*n_ai_traces fig.update_layout( title="PCA Visualization — Colored by Cluster", xaxis_title="Overall Seniority Score (Experience + Education)", yaxis_title="Education-Experience Balance", font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), height=520, updatemenus=[dict( type="dropdown", direction="down", x=1.0, xanchor="right", y=1.18, yanchor="top", buttons=[ dict(label="Color by Cluster", method="update", args=[{"visible": cluster_visibility}, {"title": "PCA Visualization — Colored by Cluster"}]), dict(label="Color by AI Job Status", method="update", args=[{"visible": ai_visibility}, {"title": "PCA Visualization — Colored by AI Job Status"}]), ] )] ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Explained variance (PC1, PC2): [0.5202318197128315,0.4797681802871685] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Insight:** The 2D PCA projection shows reasonably distinct groupings between clusters, confirming that the KMeans solution captures real structure in the data rather than arbitrary partitions. Switching the view to AI Job Status shows that AI-related postings are dispersed throughout the lower-experience region of the projection rather than forming their own isolated cluster — consistent with AI skills appearing across many traditional job categories rather than as a separate occupational class. ## Classification Models Two supervised models are trained to predict whether a job posting is AI-related, using experience, education, and occupational classification as features. Since AI-related jobs make up only ~28% of postings, **class weights are computed and applied** (equivalent to scikit-learn's `class_weight="balanced"`) to prevent the models from defaulting to the majority class. ::: {#1d5f8260 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} features = ["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE", "MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN", "SOC_ENC", "ONET_ENC"] assembler2 = VectorAssembler(inputCols=features, outputCol="features_raw2") sdf_feat = assembler2.transform(sdf_clustered) scaler2 = StandardScaler(inputCol="features_raw2", outputCol="features_scaled2", withMean=True, withStd=True) scaler2_model = scaler2.fit(sdf_feat) sdf_feat_scaled = scaler2_model.transform(sdf_feat) train_df, test_df = sdf_feat_scaled.randomSplit([0.8, 0.2], seed=42) counts = {row["AI_JOB"]: row["count"] for row in train_df.groupBy("AI_JOB").count().collect()} total = sum(counts.values()) w0 = total / (2 * counts[0]) w1 = total / (2 * counts[1]) train_df = train_df.withColumn("weight", when(col("AI_JOB") == 1, w1).otherwise(w0)) print(f"Class weights -> Non-AI: {w0:.3f}, AI-Related: {w1:.3f}") lr = LogisticRegression(featuresCol="features_scaled2", labelCol="AI_JOB", weightCol="weight", maxIter=1000) lr_model = lr.fit(train_df) lr_pred = lr_model.transform(test_df).select("AI_JOB", "prediction").toPandas() rf = RandomForestClassifier(featuresCol="features_raw2", labelCol="AI_JOB", weightCol="weight", numTrees=100, seed=42) rf_model = rf.fit(train_df) rf_pred = rf_model.transform(test_df).select("AI_JOB", "prediction").toPandas() print("\n=== Logistic Regression ===") print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(lr_pred['AI_JOB'], lr_pred['prediction']):.4f}") print(f"F1 Score: {f1_score(lr_pred['AI_JOB'], lr_pred['prediction']):.4f}") print("\n=== Random Forest ===") print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(rf_pred['AI_JOB'], rf_pred['prediction']):.4f}") print(f"F1 Score: {f1_score(rf_pred['AI_JOB'], rf_pred['prediction']):.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Class weights -> Non-AI: 0.699, AI-Related: 1.757 === Logistic Regression === Accuracy: 0.6744 F1 Score: 0.4254 === Random Forest === Accuracy: 0.6774 F1 Score: 0.4267 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#e3b629cd .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} results = { "Logistic Regression": confusion_matrix(lr_pred['AI_JOB'], lr_pred['prediction']), "Random Forest": confusion_matrix(rf_pred['AI_JOB'], rf_pred['prediction']) } for model_name, cm in results.items(): fig = px.imshow( cm, text_auto=True, labels=dict(x="Predicted", y="Actual", color="Count"), x=["Non-AI", "AI-Related"], y=["Non-AI", "AI-Related"], title=f"Confusion Matrix - {model_name}", color_continuous_scale="Blues" ) fig.update_layout( font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), height=400 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Insight:** With balanced class weights and corrected education data, both models achieve ~67% accuracy and F1 scores around 0.43. Random Forest slightly outperforms Logistic Regression, suggesting modest nonlinear relationships in the data. The improvement over the uncorrected education feature confirms that fixing the placeholder values produced a cleaner, more reliable signal. ::: {#90ade28d .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} importance_df = pd.DataFrame({ "Feature": features, "Importance": rf_model.featureImportances.toArray() }).sort_values("Importance", ascending=False) print(importance_df) fig = px.bar( importance_df, x="Importance", y="Feature", orientation="h", title="Random Forest Feature Importance", labels={"Importance": "Importance Score", "Feature": "Feature"}, color="Importance", color_continuous_scale="Reds" ) fig.update_layout( font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), height=400 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Feature Importance 0 MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE 0.885126 1 MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN 0.114874 2 SOC_ENC 0.000000 3 ONET_ENC 0.000000 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Insight:** Years of experience is overwhelmingly the strongest predictor of AI job classification (importance: 0.885), with education contributing a much smaller share (0.115). Occupational classification codes (SOC, ONET) contribute almost nothing once experience and education are accounted for — reinforcing the clustering finding that career stage, not job title taxonomy, differentiates AI roles. ::: {#3cad2763 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} edu_ai = sdf_clustered.groupBy("MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN").agg( avg("AI_JOB").alias("Proportion_AI") ).toPandas() edu_ai.columns = ["Min Education Level", "Proportion AI Jobs"] edu_ai = edu_ai.sort_values("Min Education Level") fig = px.bar( edu_ai, x="Min Education Level", y="Proportion AI Jobs", title="Proportion of AI Job Postings by Minimum Education Level", labels={"Min Education Level": "Education Level Code", "Proportion AI Jobs": "Proportion of AI Jobs"}, color="Proportion AI Jobs", color_continuous_scale="Oranges" ) fig.update_layout( font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), height=400 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Insight:** AI job proportion varies across education levels, though the spike at the median-imputed level (2.0, ~Bachelor's) partly reflects records that originally had no education requirement listed. Even accounting for this, postings with at least a Bachelor's degree show meaningfully higher AI density than those requiring only a high school diploma or equivalent. ## Summary This ML analysis extends the EDA by applying PySpark MLlib clustering and classification models to the AI vs. Non-AI career question. **Key findings:** - AI-related jobs represent approximately 28% of postings after filtering invalid placeholder records, confirming that AI has broadly permeated the labor market beyond a narrow technical niche - A data quality issue was identified and corrected: the education field used code 99 as a "missing data" flag, which was distorting both clustering and classification results - The elbow method and silhouette score jointly support **k=3** as the optimal number of clusters, yielding interpretable groups differentiated primarily by years of experience - AI job density is highest among lower-experience clusters (~30%) and lowest among senior/high-experience roles (10.9%), suggesting AI roles concentrate earlier in career trajectories - Logistic Regression and Random Forest achieve ~67% accuracy and F1 scores of ~0.43 after correcting the education feature and applying balanced class weights - Years of experience is by far the dominant predictor of AI job classification (88.5% importance), far outweighing education (11.5%) and occupational codes (~0%) **Recommendations for job seekers:** - Early-to-mid career professionals are well-positioned to enter AI-adjacent roles, since AI job density is highest in lower-experience clusters - Formal education level matters less than expected — occupational and skills alignment appear more important than degree level alone - Build demonstrable experience with data science, analytics, or ML tools early in one's career, since experience — not credentials — is the strongest signal in this analysis - Target industries like Professional Services, Finance, and Information Technology where AI hiring is most concentrated
